lessons.title: A container from scratch: rootfs, namespaces, cgroup
lessons.goal:
Build a container without Docker's runtime: a root file system, new namespaces, and a cgroup, then compare with what Docker creates.

Why it matters: once you can do this, you can debug any container runtime, explain the isolation limits honestly, and see why "containers share the host kernel" has security consequences.

setup.note: These steps use sudo and Docker only to obtain an Alpine root file system, then build a container **by hand**. They remove everything at the end. Needs Docker (or any way to get a root file system tarball).
commands: sudo docker rm -f lab-d >/dev/null 2>&1; sudo systemctl stop lab-ctr 2>/dev/null; sudo systemctl reset-failed lab-ctr 2>/dev/null; sudo rm -rf /tmp/lab/rootfs; true

steps.title: Step 1: a root file system
steps.text: A container image is mostly a tarball of a small Linux root file system. We take Alpine's from Docker (`export` writes a container's files as a tar stream).

run.cmd: mkdir rootfs; id=$(sudo docker create alpine); sudo docker export $id | sudo tar -x -C rootfs; sudo docker rm $id > /dev/null
ls rootfs | tr '\n' ' '; echo
run.output: bin dev etc home lib media mnt opt proc root run sbin srv sys tmp usr var

run.cmd: head -n 2 rootfs/etc/os-release | cut -d= -f2 | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.title: Step 2: chroot changes the root directory
steps.text: `chroot DIR CMD` makes DIR the root for the command. The program now sees Alpine's files instead of ours: a different distribution, same kernel. But it still sees the host's processes, network and hostname.

run.cmd: sudo chroot rootfs /bin/sh -c 'head -n 1 /etc/os-release; ls / | wc -l | awk "{print \$1, \"entries in /\"}"'
sudo chroot rootfs /bin/sh -c 'uname -sr | cut -d- -f1'; uname -sr | cut -d- -f1

steps.after: The kernel version is identical inside and outside: **there is no second kernel**.

steps.title: Step 3: add the namespaces
steps.text: Now isolate what the process can see: new mount, UTS (hostname), IPC, network and PID namespaces, and inside mount a fresh `/proc` so `ps` shows only our view.

run.cmd: sudo unshare --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid --fork chroot rootfs /bin/sh -c 'mount -t proc proc /proc; hostname lab-ctr; echo "hostname: $(hostname)"; echo "my pid: $$"; echo "processes visible: $(ps | tail -n +2 | wc -l)"; echo "network links: $(ip -o link | wc -l)"'
run.output:
hostname: lab-ctr
my pid: 1
processes visible: 3
network links: 1

steps.under: This is the essence of `docker run`: `clone()` with the namespace flags, `pivot_root`/`chroot` into the image, mount `/proc`, `/sys` and `/dev`, set up network (a veth pair joined to a bridge), then `exec` the command. runc does exactly this, driven by a JSON `config.json`.

steps.title: Step 4: a cgroup for limits
steps.text: We run the container as a transient systemd service so that systemd creates its cgroup, and give it a memory limit. From the host we then look at the processes, the cgroup and what the root of the process is.

run.cmd: sudo systemd-run --unit=lab-ctr -q -p MemoryMax=30M unshare --mount --uts --pid --fork chroot /tmp/lab/rootfs /bin/sleep 60; sleep 1; systemctl show lab-ctr -p MemoryMax | tr '\n' ' '; echo
cat /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/lab-ctr.service/cgroup.procs | wc -l | awk '{print $1, "processes in the container cgroup"}'
p=$(tail -n 1 /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/lab-ctr.service/cgroup.procs); sudo readlink /proc/$p/root; sudo cat /proc/$p/comm

steps.after: From the host the container's `sleep` is a normal process: it has a host PID, lives in the cgroup, and its root directory is our `rootfs`. Nothing hides it from the host.

steps.title: Compare with Docker's container
steps.text: `docker run` adds image layers, a network bridge and many defaults, but uses the same kernel features. We start one with limits and read its cgroup files.

run.cmd: sudo docker run -d --name lab-d --hostname lab-docker --memory 30m --cpus 0.5 alpine sleep 60 > /dev/null; sleep 1; pid=$(sudo docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' lab-d); sudo ls /proc/$pid/ns | tr '\n' ' '; echo
run.output: cgroup ipc mnt net pid pid_for_children time time_for_children user uts

run.cmd: pid=$(sudo docker inspect -f '{{.State.Pid}}' lab-d); cg=$(sudo cat /proc/$pid/cgroup | cut -d: -f3); echo "memory.max: $(cat /sys/fs/cgroup$cg/memory.max)"; echo "cpu.max: $(cat /sys/fs/cgroup$cg/cpu.max)"

steps.under: `--memory 30m` became `memory.max = 31457280` and `--cpus 0.5` became `cpu.max = 50000 100000`. Docker is a convenient front end that writes these files and sets up namespaces. This also shows why container isolation is weaker than VM isolation: a kernel vulnerability reachable from inside is a host vulnerability.

steps.title: Clean up
steps.text: Stop both containers and delete the root file system.

run.cmd: sudo docker rm -f lab-d > /dev/null; sudo systemctl stop lab-ctr; sudo rm -rf rootfs; echo cleaned

quiz.q: Which statement about containers is correct?
options: Each container runs its own kernel
Containers share the host kernel and are isolated by namespaces and cgroups
quiz.explain: Step 2: same kernel version inside and outside.

quiz.q: What does `docker run --memory 30m` end up as?

options: The view of the file system root only
quiz.explain: It is not a security boundary by itself.

quiz.q: Which tool in Docker's stack performs the namespace and cgroup setup?

check.scenario: A security review asks: "a root process in a container escapes. What are the consequences compared with a VM?" Answer in terms of what you built.
check.answer: A container is a process on the **host kernel**. If root in the container finds a kernel bug (or has too many capabilities, a mounted Docker socket or `--privileged`), it can reach the host and all other containers, which share that kernel. A VM escape must break the hypervisor and virtual device emulation, a much smaller attack surface. Mitigate with rootless containers, dropped capabilities, seccomp, SELinux/AppArmor, read-only roots and user namespaces.

lessons.title: Rootless containers and image layers
lessons.goal:
Create mount, PID and user namespaces as an **ordinary user**, and build an image-style layered file system with `overlayfs` by hand.

Why it matters: rootless containers (Podman, rootless Docker) are the safer default, and layered images explain why pulling is fast, why images are read-only, and why deleting a file in a layer does not shrink the image.

setup.note: Overlay mounts need sudo. The user-namespace steps need no root. Everything is removed at the end.

steps.title: Namespaces without root
steps.text: A **user namespace** lets an unprivileged user become UID 0 *inside*. In that namespace the user may create mount and PID namespaces and mount a tmpfs, because the privileges apply only to namespace-owned resources. No sudo.

run.cmd: unshare --user --map-root-user --mount --pid --fork --mount-proc sh -c 'echo "uid inside: $(id -u)"; mount -t tmpfs tmpfs /mnt && echo "mounted a tmpfs as an ordinary user"; echo "processes visible: $(ps -e | tail -n +2 | wc -l)"'
run.output:
uid inside: 0
mounted a tmpfs as an ordinary user
processes visible: 5

steps.title: The ID mapping
steps.text: Only your own UID is mapped (to 0). Files owned by anyone else show up as `nobody` inside, and you cannot become another user. Real rootless runtimes use `newuidmap` and the ranges in `/etc/subuid` to map thousands of IDs.

run.cmd: unshare -Ur sh -c 'cat /proc/self/uid_map | tr -s " " " "; ls -ln /etc/passwd | awk "{print \"/etc/passwd owner inside: \", \$3}"'
grep -c '^opc:' /etc/subuid 2>/dev/null; sysctl user.max_user_namespaces | tr -s ' ' ' '

steps.after: `0 1000 1` reads: UID 0 inside = UID 1000 outside, 1 ID long. `/etc/passwd` belongs to root (UID 0 outside), which is **not mapped**, so it appears as 65534 (`nobody`).

steps.title: Image layers with overlayfs
steps.text: A container image is a stack of read-only **layers**. **overlayfs** merges `lowerdir` (read-only) with an `upperdir` (the writable layer) into a `merged` view. Writes go to the upper layer (**copy-up**); the lower stays untouched, so many containers share one image.

run.cmd: mkdir lower upper work merged; echo base > lower/base.txt; echo old > lower/config.txt
sudo mount -t overlay overlay -o lowerdir=lower,upperdir=upper,workdir=work merged; ls merged | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.title: Writes land in the upper layer
steps.text: We modify one file and create another through the merged view.

run.cmd: echo new > merged/config.txt; echo extra > merged/added.txt
echo "lower: $(cat lower/config.txt)  merged: $(cat merged/config.txt)"
ls upper | tr '\n' ' '; echo

steps.title: Deleting makes a whiteout
steps.text: Removing a file from a lower layer cannot change the lower layer. overlayfs creates a **whiteout**: a character device with number 0/0 in the upper layer that hides the name. That is why deleting a big file in a later Dockerfile layer does not make the image smaller.

run.cmd: rm merged/base.txt; ls merged | tr '\n' ' '; ls lower | tr '\n' ' '; echo
ls -l upper/base.txt | cut -c1-10; stat -c 'device %t:%T' upper/base.txt

steps.under: Docker keeps image layers under `/var/lib/docker/overlay2`, one directory per layer, and mounts them as `lowerdir=layerN:layerN-1:...` with a per-container upper layer. `docker commit` or `build` turns an upper layer into a new lower layer. Pulling shares layers that are already present, by their content hash.

run.cmd: sudo umount merged; sudo rm -rf lower upper work merged; echo cleaned

quiz.q: Why can an unprivileged user create a mount namespace inside a user namespace?
options: The privileges apply only to resources owned by the namespace
quiz.explain: Capabilities in a user namespace are scoped to it.

quiz.q: What is a whiteout in overlayfs?
options: A 0/0 character device in the upper layer that hides a lower file

quiz.q: Why does deleting a file in a later image layer not shrink the image?
options: The data stays in the earlier, read-only layer
Ranges of extra UIDs a user may map in user namespaces

check.scenario: Why would you run containers rootless, and what limits do you accept?
check.answer: A container escape lands as an ordinary user, not root, and a compromised runtime cannot take over the host. Accept: no binding to ports below 1024 without a sysctl or proxy, slower networking (slirp4netns/pasta), restricted features (some filesystems, `ping` needs sysctl), and the need for subuid/subgid ranges.

interview.a: A process in new namespaces and a cgroup, with a root file system from an image. It shares the host kernel. See [the lesson](#/lesson/39/container-by-hand).

interview.q: How is a container different from a VM?
interview.a: A VM has its own kernel on virtual hardware under a hypervisor; a container shares the host kernel. Containers start faster and are lighter but isolate less.

interview.q: What does docker run actually set up?
interview.a: Namespaces (pid, net, mnt, uts, ipc, optionally user), a cgroup with limits, a root file system from layered image storage (overlayfs), network (veth + bridge/NAT), capabilities, seccomp and LSM profiles.
Containers run by an unprivileged user using user namespaces, so a breakout does not give root on the host. See [the lesson](#/lesson/39/rootless-and-layers).

interview.q: Why does deleting a file in a Dockerfile layer not reduce image size?
interview.a: Layers are read-only and stacked; deletion adds a whiteout in a new layer while the data stays in the old one.

interview.q: How do you find a container's cgroup limits from the host?
interview.a: Get its host PID (`docker inspect`), read `/proc/PID/cgroup`, then `memory.max`, `cpu.max` in that cgroup directory.

glossary.def: A process isolated by namespaces and limited by cgroups, running from an image's root file system.
A read-only file system layer; images are stacks of layers.
A union file system that merges a read-only lower layer with a writable upper layer.
A marker in an upper layer that hides a file of a lower layer.
The reference OCI runtime that creates containers from a config.json.
A container run by an unprivileged user via user namespaces.
